meta_desc: Class 5 maths shapes and angles made simple: types of angles, comparing sizes and angles in shapes, with worked case studies and a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: Acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex — NCERT Class 5 Chapter 2 packs a lot into one word: angle. Here is a plain-language walkthrough of the whole chapter, two worked case studies, and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Open a pair of scissors a little and you have made a small angle; open them wide and the angle grows. That single picture is the heart of class 5 maths shapes and angles, NCERT Chapter 2. An angle is not the length of the two arms — a big scissors and a small scissors opened the same amount make the same angle. Ten-year-olds trip on this constantly, so it is worth fixing on day one: an angle measures the turn between two lines that meet at a point, nothing else.

The chapter asks children to do three connected things: name the different kinds of angles, compare and estimate how big an angle is, and then hunt for angles inside everyday shapes. I will take each in turn, keep the language plain, and finish with two real-life case studies of the kind the NCERT chapter loves.

The five types of angles in class 5 maths shapes and angles

An angle is measured in degrees, written with the small circle symbol, so a quarter turn is 90°. Chapter 2 introduces five names. Learn them by the size of the turn, not by memorising a list.

AngleSizeEveryday example
AcuteLess than 90°An open pair of scissors, a slice of pizza
RightExactly 90°The corner of a book or a window
ObtuseBetween 90° and 180°A reclining chair, an open laptop
StraightExactly 180°A flat, straight line — a see-saw balanced level
ReflexBetween 180° and 360°The larger angle on the outside of an L-shaped corner

The right angle is the anchor. Once a child can spot 90° on sight — the corner of a notebook is a perfect checker — every other angle is judged against it. Smaller than the corner? Acute. Bigger, but not yet a flat line? Obtuse.

The reflex angle catches everyone

Reflex is the one that trips students. When two lines meet, they actually make two angles: the smaller one you notice first, and the big one going the long way round. If the small angle is 70°, the reflex angle beside it is 360° − 70° = 290°. The two together complete a full turn of 360°. In my experience teaching this, drawing both arcs in different colours is what finally makes it click.

Comparing and estimating angle sizes

NCERT is clever here: before children ever touch a protractor, the chapter asks them to estimate. Is this angle nearer to a right angle, or nearer to a straight line? That guess-first habit builds real number sense. A few anchor values are worth memorising as reference points.

  • A full turn all the way around is 360°.
  • Half a turn — a straight line — is 180°.
  • A quarter turn — a square corner — is 90°.
  • Half of a right angle is 45°, roughly the tilt of a book leaning on a shelf.

To compare two angles without measuring, children learn a neat trick: trace one angle on tracing paper and lay it over the other so the arms and corner match. Whichever angle’s second arm sticks out further is the bigger one. It proves, physically, that arm length has nothing to do with angle size.

Angles inside shapes

The final part of the chapter turns detective. A triangle has three angles, a rectangle has four (all right angles), and the children go looking. A key discovery the NCERT activities push toward: the three angles of any triangle always add up to 180°. You can show this by tearing the three corners off a paper triangle and fitting them together — they line up into a straight line every time. That hands-on proof beats any rule written on a board.

Rigid shapes matter too. A triangle keeps its shape when you push it; a rectangle collapses into a slanted parallelogram. That is why bridges and cycle frames are built from triangles — a genuinely useful, non-obvious fact that Chapter 2 hints at through its shape activities.

Case study 1: The clock on the classroom wall

Here is the kind of passage the case-study e-book uses. Riya looks at the wall clock. The face is a circle, and the two hands meet at the centre, making an angle between them. At 3 o’clock the hour hand points to 3 and the minute hand points to 12.

  • What angle do the hands make at 3 o’clock? From 12 to 3 is a quarter of the full clock face. A full turn is 360°, so a quarter is 90°. The hands make a right angle.
  • Is the angle at 1 o’clock acute or obtuse? From 12 to 1 is a small turn, far less than a square corner, so it is acute (it is 30°, since each hour mark is 360° ÷ 12 = 30°).
  • At 6 o’clock, what kind of angle do the hands make? The hands point exactly opposite each other, forming a straight line — a straight angle of 180°.

Case study 2: Folding a paper fan

Arjun folds a rectangular sheet into a paper fan. Each fold is a straight crease, and when he opens the fan a little, the outer edges make an angle. When the fan is barely open the angle is acute; open halfway and it may reach a right angle; opened right out flat, the two ends make a straight angle of 180°. The lovely part is that the paper never changes length — only the turn between the ends grows. It is the scissors idea again, and pointing that connection out helps the whole chapter hang together.

quiz.title: Class 5 Shapes and Angles Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on the five types of angles, comparing sizes and angles inside shapes. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: NCERT Class 5 Maths Chapter 2 — Shapes and Angles

questions.q: An angle that is less than 90° is called:
questions.explanation: Any angle smaller than a square corner (90°) is an acute angle.

questions.q: The corner of a notebook is an example of a:
questions.explanation: A perfect square corner is exactly 90°, which is a right angle.

questions.q: How many degrees are there in a full turn all the way around?
questions.explanation: A complete turn is 360°. Half a turn is 180° and a quarter turn is 90°.
It is more than 90° but less than 180°, so it is obtuse.

questions.q: At 6 o’clock the two hands of a clock make a:
questions.explanation: The hands point exactly opposite, forming a straight line of 180°.

questions.q: The three angles of any triangle add up to:
questions.explanation: The angles of every triangle always total 180°.

questions.q: Two lines meet and the small angle is 80°. The reflex angle beside it is:
questions.explanation: The two angles complete a full turn: 360° − 80° = 280°.

questions.q: A big pair of scissors and a small pair are opened the same amount. Their angles are:
options: The big scissors’ angle is bigger
The small scissors’ angle is bigger
questions.explanation: An angle measures the turn, not the arm length, so both angles are equal.

faq.q: What is NCERT Class 5 Maths Chapter 2 about?
faq.a: Chapter 2, Shapes and Angles, teaches what an angle is, the five types (acute, right, obtuse, straight and reflex), how to compare and estimate angle sizes, and how to find angles inside shapes like triangles and rectangles.

faq.q: What are the five types of angles a Class 5 student should know?
faq.a: Acute (less than 90°), right (exactly 90°), obtuse (between 90° and 180°), straight (exactly 180°) and reflex (between 180° and 360°). The right angle is the anchor everything else is compared against.

faq.q: Does the length of the arms change the size of an angle?
faq.a: No. An angle measures only the amount of turn between two lines meeting at a point. Long arms or short arms make no difference — the scissors opened the same amount give the same angle either way.

faq.q: How can a child compare two angles without a protractor?
faq.a: Trace one angle on paper, then lay it over the second so the corner and one arm match. Whichever angle’s other arm opens out further is the larger one — a simple hands-on way NCERT encourages before measuring.
